title: Fine bodies, empty words
hookLine: their bodies impress you and their speech charms you, but they're like propped-up timber (63:4)

lines: A STREET ON A FILM SET.
cards: Walk through a film set and you'll see a whole street: shop fronts, balconies, a church tower. Walk around the back and it's plywood and scaffolding, held up by diagonal beams. From the front, perfect.
From behind, nothing. Surah sixty-three is about people in Medina who were a little like that street. It's named for them, Al-Munafiqun, and in one verse it gives them an image that's hard to forget.

teach.b: Verse four. Pickthall: "And when thou seest them their figures please thee; and if they speak thou givest ear unto their speech. (They are) as though they were blocks of wood in striped cloaks."

The Arabic image is khushubun musannadah: timber propped up against a wall. Wood that looks solid but can't stand on its own, with nothing living in it. Fine bodies, polished words, and inside, no root.
The word for what the surah describes is nifaq.

teach.h: NIFAQ: A BURROW WITH TWO DOORS.
teach.b: Classical Arabic dictionaries connect it to the nafiqa', a burrow some desert animals dig with a hidden second exit: one way in that everyone sees, another way out that no one does. Nifaq is having two doors.
In the Qur'an, the munafiqun are people who declared faith in Medina while working against the community in secret. But the hadith also turns the word into a mirror for believers.
Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ naming the signs: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; when he's trusted, he betrays. And Muslim records a tender scene.
Abu Bakr met a companion named Hanzala and asked how he was. Hanzala answered: Hanzala has become a hypocrite!
With the Prophet, he said, he felt paradise and hell before his eyes; at home with his wife and children, he forgot. Abu Bakr said, I feel the same.
They went to the Prophet, who told them: if you stayed always as you are with me, angels would shake your hands in the street.

teach.h: HANZALA: AN HOUR AND AN HOUR.
teach.b: But Hanzala, an hour and an hour. Here, the worry about being two-faced isn't treated as nifaq. It's answered gently.

how: Muslim teachers often use the signs of the hypocrite from the hadith as a checklist for self-examination, and the story of Hanzala is told to reassure believers that changing moods are not hypocrisy.

o: open rejection of faith, said out loud
hypocrisy: a fine front with nothing behind it
a passing doubt that creeps in during prayer

games.q: nifaq in Al-Munafiqun — tap the pairs.
p: a burrow with a hidden exit

s: Hanzala's fear of being two-faced was itself a sign of hypocrisy
the Prophet reassured him: an hour and an hour.
the hadith names lying, breaking promises and betraying trust as signs of a hypocrite
the verse says the hypocrites looked unimpressive
their bodies please you and their speech holds your ear.

games.q: Hanzala comes to the Prophet: with you I feel paradise and hell; at home I forget. have I become a hypocrite?
o: yes; you must leave your family.
if you stayed as you are with me, angels would shake your hands; but an hour and an hour.
only scholars can feel that way all the time.
games.why: the Prophet reassured him: no one stays at that height all the time. an hour and an hour.

practice: Gently, without harshness, look at one place where your outside and inside don't match: a face you wear in one room and not another. Don't scold yourself; Hanzala's worry was met with gentleness.
Just name it, and choose one small way to bring the two sides a little closer.

wordCard.voice: Nifaq. Hypocrisy: a burrow with two doors, a fine front with timber propped up behind it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: nifaq, hypocrisy. munafiqun are those who practice it; dictionaries link the root to a burrow with two exits.

carryVoice: Your line: not propped up. Roots matter more than the front. Day six hundred twenty-eight, complete.

sources.q: And when thou seest them their figures please thee; and if they speak thou givest ear unto their speech. (They are) as though they were blocks of wood in striped cloaks.
